<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and clashed cleanly, but A (CON) controlled the decisive comparison. A's core asymmetry claim — a deployment ban binds the compliant and leaves the dangerous untouched — survived every attack. B's best pressure (B3.1: "your liability regime needs the same treaty cooperation") was the single sharpest question of the debate, and A answered it directly and persuasively at A4.1–A4.2: unilateral regulation (procurement standards, testing, strict liability up one's own chain) improves outcomes the day it is adopted with no signatures required, whereas unilateral prohibition only produces a handicap. B never rebutted that distinction; the closing merely re-labelled it ("renaming prohibition's tools as regulation") and pivoted to "prevention beats litigation," which A immediately answered by noting prohibition prevents nothing in capitals that never signed. A also turned B's own cluster-munitions precedent (major powers non-signatories, both sides using them in Ukraine) and dismantled the bioweapons analogy on incentive rather than norm — a genuinely damaging move. A's strict-liability answer to the emergent-failure-modes point (strict liability exists precisely for unforeseeable harm) went essentially unanswered. B did land real hits: the "better sensors for a human, not removal of the veto" reframe, the clean operational definition of meaningful human control (target or target class designated ex ante), and the demand for a deployed human-targeting example, which forced an honest concession from A that the hard cases are prospective. B's closing embrace of the narrow horn of A's squeeze ("that's the ban working") was a legitimate deontological stand, but it declined to engage A's civilian-cost comparison rather than defeating it. A's two clipped, over-length turns are a real execution cost, and B's tighter speeches were efficient; B also cited nonexistent reference ids ([C1.5], [C2.7]) twice. Those costs narrow but do not erase A's edge on the live enforcement and humanitarian comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure question that A's liability regime faces the identical non-compliance asymmetry, and A's answer distinguishing unilateral regulation (works alone, improves your own systems) from unilateral prohibition (works only if universal, otherwise pure handicap). That exchange was the hinge, and A's reply was the cleanest, least-answered move in the debate.</best_rebuttal>
